title: Schiffman's control of the Apollo circuit and the West End Theater
summary: She recounts how Schiffman shut a rival theater by cutting off acts, which owed him money and needed his booking.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: But I do know that we played the Apollo and the Howard in Washington, D. C., and the Royal in Baltimore.
In about 1946 -- '45 or '46 when I first moved up here in the neighborhood, there was a theater up on Boston Road near here. The McKinley Theater -- which previously had presented some revues.
I remember that Avon Long and Billie Holiday and a lot of the artists had appeared. They even did some so-called legitimate productions up
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

there. But when I moved up, the theater was practically closed. But there was an owner that tried to get some shows going there, and I appeared on the bill with Clyde Bernhardt and his orchestra, plus a couple of other acts -- comedians.
And the manager couldn't proceed with his plans because Schiffman had things pretty well sewed up.
And the manager couldn't get any movies to show because that was to be a combination movie and vaudeville house.
Yes.
So he had to close.
And there was another instance in which Schiffman had a lot to do with closing the theater. A theater on 125th Street opened, say, diagonally across from the Apollo Theater called "The West End."
And it opened with Benny Carter and a group of dancers -- chorus girls -- and some of the comedians and some of the acts that played the Apollo Theater.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

But Schiffman didn't want the competition, so he mentioned to the -- some of the comedians and some of the acts who had worked at The West End, that if they played The West End, that they couldn't play the Apollo.
What was the name of the theater?
The West End, that was the name of the theater. That they couldn't work at the Apollo for him anymore.
So this sort of made a shortage of acts. And so The West End after about three or four weeks. It couldn't stay opened under the circumstances.

I found this sort of difficult to understand why it was necessary to close the theater, and why or how, because he had threatened several of the acts that if they played there, they couldn't play the Apollo, when there was no ongoing production at the Apollo.
I mean, every act that was in there was just in there for a week. But I could only conclude that maybe some of the acts might've owed Schiffman
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
some money. Maybe they borrowed when they weren't working.
Gave them advances somewhat.

Yeah, and I feel that they were indebted to him in some kind of way. But they certainly didn't make themselves available for The West End. And so The West End had to close. And I also I understood that --
You think there might've been any stronger threat than that?
I doubt it. I wasn't necessary to make any stronger threats. I mean the threat was that there was going to be a shortage of acts.

And, of course, although there were just these acts that appeared in the Apollo, that were told, when you consider that there's a possibility that his influence -- Schiffman's influence went farther than that, perhaps even into the TOBA circuit. And a lot of artists were involved then in -- He could've arranged it so that they wouldn't be able to work in any of the theaters. So

this would be cutting off their source of income. So this was -- I do know that The West End closed in a matter of three or four weeks, or less than that.
